P01.author: A
P01.explanation: "Blockaded" fits: warships across the harbor mouth turned back every freighter, so the alliance cut the port off from all shipping. "Boycotted" fails because the alliance's own wool buyers sent ships that were turned back too; the buyers had not stopped buying, the port was simply closed to everyone. "Bombarded" fails because the waterfront sheds still stand, holding the unsold bales. "Annexed" fails because the island's flag still flew over the customs house and the island's own clerks still ran it.

P02.author: E
P02.explanation: All twenty-eight crew went down with the ship, their bodies were never recovered, and the hatches were still battened decades later, so the sealed hull still holds its dead: a "tomb." A "strongbox" keeps valuables secure, but the sealed hull carried only ballast. A "trellis" is a framework things grow along, but its plates are bare of growth. A "tripwire" is a hidden hazard that catches the unwary, but it lies in ninety feet of water and ferries pass over it twice a day.

P03.author: A
P03.explanation: "Bulldozed" fits: within a year the church's site was a parking lot and its stones were rubble dumped in a marsh, so the council had it knocked down. "Condemned" fails because engineers found the walls sound and the tower true, so there was no finding that the building was unsafe. "Crated" fails because the stones were broken into rubble and dumped, not numbered and shipped to be rebuilt. "Commandeered" fails because the council made no use of the building; it put a parking lot where it stood.

P04.author: B
P04.explanation: A celebrated actress recited the poems in sold-out halls across the country and cheap editions followed her from city to city, so her poems had been "popularized": carried to a wide public. "Pirated" fails because each cheap edition carried her printer's license and paid her share of every copy, so none was printed without leave. "Plagiarized" fails because the actress named the poet each night. "Panned" fails because the city papers had named two of the poems among the season's best.

P05.author: C
P05.explanation: "Dike" fits: the wall stands on the riverbank footed below the waterline, and each spring the river rises nearly to its top and floods the meadows on either side, so the wall is what holds the river off the orchard. "Hearth" fails because frost blackens the blossom on the trees beside the wall as much as on any other, so the wall gives no warmth. "Fence" fails because the orchard's north side lies open to the pasture, so the wall closes off only the river side. "Firebreak" fails because the village fire died out in the pasture on the orchard's open north side; the wall stands on the far, river side and never met it.

P06.author: D
P06.explanation: The treasury bought a controlling share of all four papers and the war minister named their editors, so the government "nationalized" the press, taking it into state ownership. "Muzzled" fails because no official read the pages before printing and the papers went on attacking the ministers who owned them, so they were not silenced. "Mobilized" fails because the papers refused the ministry's recruiting notices, so their new owner did not enlist them in the war effort. "Impoverished" fails because treasury money let the papers double their pages.

P07.author: D
P07.explanation: The ice was frozen to the ground and left the meadows' old soil in place, while the river beneath it cut a slot two hundred feet deep into the granite, so the glacier "incised" the valley floor: it cut a narrow channel into it and left the rest alone. "Milled" fails because the meadow soil, with its pollen older than the ice, survived under the glacier, so the ice did not grind the floor down. "Mantled" fails because that same old soil is still at the surface, so nothing was laid over the floor. "Littered" fails because all the rock the ice carried lies heaped in one ridge across the valley's mouth, not scattered over the floor.

P08.author: D
P08.explanation: The marsh sheds a steady drift of shredded grass on every ebb, and the shrimp just outside its channel were full of that grass, so the marsh is the bay's "kitchen": the place where the bay's animals' food is made. "Kidney" fails because the water left carrying as much fertilizer nitrate as the creek brought in, so the marsh removed none of that waste. "Net" fails because the water ran out just as brown with mud as it came in, so the marsh caught nothing from it. "Lung" fails because the outgoing water held the same oxygen as the bay.

P09.author: E
P09.explanation: The swells broke along the bar while boats moored behind it at the piers survived storms that wrecked boats on the open coast, so the bar sheltered the harbor from the sea: a "seawall." A "tollbooth" is a point where everyone passing must pay, but ships steered over without a pilot along publicly buoyed water, so crossing cost them nothing. A "turnstile" admits traffic one at a time, but ships crossed several abreast on every high tide. A "wharf" is where cargo is loaded and unloaded, but the ships crossed the bar and unloaded at the town's piers.

P10.author: B
P10.explanation: The tablet records the barley one farmer brought in, day by day, under the storehouse keeper's seal, and it was kept in the farmer's own house among his sealed tablets, so it is his "receipt": the receiver's sealed acknowledgment of what he delivered. "Payroll" fails because the barley here flows in from a farmer to the storehouse, not out to a list of workers as pay. "Recipe" fails because the lines are dated deliveries, not ingredients or steps. "Roadmap" fails because every line is a delivery by one farmer to the same storehouse on a day of one month, so the days mark dates, not stages of a journey.

P11.author: D
P11.explanation: The dunes buried every road across the basin, so the village could be reached only by a three-day walk, while its families went on living in a hollow among them: the sand had "imprisoned" it, shutting it in. "Nibbled" fails because the families kept every house and date garden, so the village lost no piece of itself; what the sand took was the basin around it. "Lifted" fails because the doorways still open at their builders' height, so the village's ground never rose. "Lashed" fails because the village lay in a still hollow below dunes taller than its palms, sheltered from the wind that would drive sand against it.

P12.author: C
P12.explanation: "Fertilized" fits: a flock that visits only briefly has left the slope's soil with twice the nitrogen of the ungrazed side, and the grass there grows taller and greener, so the flock's dung has enriched the hillside. "Denuded" fails because the grazed slope carries more grass than the other side, not less. "Groomed" fails because the grass grows in tall, uneven tussocks, not a neat, even turf. "Furrowed" fails because the sheep wander in every direction and have worn no paths.

P13.author: B
P13.explanation: The meadows lost half their winter elk, the collars showed cow after cow wintering in the timber upslope, and the total barely changed, so the wolves "redistributed" the herd, moving it from meadows to timber. "Reduced" fails because the valley's total barely changed. "Rattled" fails because in the timber the elk grazed heads down as long as meadow elk had before the wolves, so they changed where they fed, not how calmly. "Rejuvenated" fails because the few elk the wolves took were mostly calves, which made the herd older.

P14.author: A
P14.explanation: "Bridge" fits: clams from two distant hot-spring fields met on the bones, and their young reached a third field, so the carcass let these clams cross the gap between springs hundreds of miles apart. "Battery" fails because the bones were bare within two years, so the carcass did not supply energy slowly over a long period. "Banquet" fails because what matters is that clams from separate fields settled and bred there and sent young onward, not a crowd feeding. "Cupboard" fails because the clams lived and bred on the bones and then moved on; no one came back to draw on stored food.

P15.author: B
P15.explanation: An earthquake shifted the land north of the fault six feet east, so the center stripe now steps sideways at the fault and the asphalt there is broken across both lanes: the surface had been "ruptured". "Raised" fails because the stakes on either side showed the roadbed still at its laid height; the land moved sideways, not up. "Rippled" fails because trucks braking at the stop sign, where folds would be shoved up, left the asphalt level. "Rutted" fails because trucks crawling up the climb, where grooves would form, also left it level.

P16.author: B
P16.explanation: The villagers walked to a spring that legend said had cured a blind shepherd, knelt, drank in turn, tied cloth to the thorn, and walked home in silence, so the walk was a "pilgrimage": a journey made to honor a holy place. "Roundup" fails because they walked home between the grazing ponies, leaving them where they were. "Pageant" fails because, though they wore their best clothes, they performed nothing for anyone; kneeling, drinking and silence are acts of devotion, not a show. "Raid" fails because the neighboring parish made the same walk to the same spring a week later, so the spring was shared, not something taken from them.

P17.author: A
P17.explanation: "Cage" fits: voles born in the strip never move more than half a mile, and each stretch has drifted genetically on its own, so the strip holds its voles in place. "Corridor" fails because nothing travels along it; the genes differ from one stretch to the next a few miles apart, which could not happen if voles moved through. "Cafeteria" fails because forest voles seldom enter the strip, and the voles there are residents born in it, not visitors coming to feed. "Cemetery" fails because strip voles live as long as forest voles.

P18.author: C
P18.explanation: "Enlarged" fits: the print keeps every feature where the survey has it but doubles every distance, harbor widths and scale bar alike, so the engraver copied the survey at a bigger size. "Doctored" fails because every cape, bay, and shoal sits where the survey puts it and the scale bar was doubled to match, so no fact was falsified. "Flipped" fails because north is at the top of both and nothing is reversed. "Gilded" fails because the print's open sea is as bare of ornament as the survey's; the extra space was filled by the coast itself.

P19.author: E
P19.explanation: The glacier can be seen from thirty miles across the plain and points at the one notch where a road crosses the ridge, and guidebooks tell drovers to walk toward it, so it shows travelers their route: it is the valley's "signpost." A "storeroom" holds supplies for later use, but in dry summers the river runs as low as the rain-fed streams, so the glacier saves no water for the dry months. A "timepiece" marks the hours, but with its meltwater going underground the river hardly changes from morning to night. A "thermometer" registers temperature changes, but the front has stood at one ledge through warm decades and cold.

P20.author: B
P20.explanation: Miners whose cabins had no stove spent their winter evenings at the store, reading newspapers aloud and playing cards by the fire while buying almost nothing, so the store was the camp's "parlor": its shared sitting room. "Pawnshop" fails because the miners paid cash for a little tobacco and pledged nothing for credit. "Repository" fails because the safe held the merchant's own takings, not anything miners deposited. "Pharmacy" fails because the bottles held whiskey.

P21.author: C
P21.explanation: "Entombed" fits: soon after the wreck a sandbar settled over the spot, the divers could find the hull only by probing down through it, and beneath it the ship lay sealed away with sound wood and intact cargo, so the seabed buried and preserved it. "Encrusted" fails because a hull covered within a few years never stood in open water long enough for shells and coral to settle, and its deck came up smooth. "Gnawed" fails because the sand shut the wood off from the water that boring creatures live in, and the planks were sound enough to hold a nail. "Dismantled" fails because, despite the drifting sand and the winter storms, the hold was intact, with casks still full of wine.

P22.author: D
P22.explanation: Winter storms rolled the ship over the rock until it broke apart, and its timbers, iron and wine jars lay strewn over a quarter mile, so the sea had "jostled" the ship, knocking it about the bottom. "Mummified" fails because a ship broken apart and scattered over a quarter mile was not preserved whole, however sound its separate timbers. "Interred" fails because the wreck lay on bare rock, where nothing could bury it. "Mined" fails because the timbers were hard and sound, worn only at the edges, not tunneled through.

P23.author: D
P23.explanation: The author's short, broken, repetitive sentences became long, balanced periods with apt variants for each repetition, so the translator "manicured" the novel, trimming and polishing its prose. "Lightened" fails because every drowning and winter of hunger is still told in full, so the polish changed how the book reads, not how dark it is. "Mutilated" fails because every chapter was kept in order. "Naturalized" fails because the family keeps its names, its fjord and its money.

P24.author: A
P24.explanation: "Capsized" fits: the squall heeled three ships until the sea poured over their rails, they did not come back up, and their crews were rescued from the upturned hulls, so the ships were overturned. "Beached" fails because this happened in mid-channel, miles from any shore. "Becalmed" fails because a squall struck the ships under full sail, so they had wind enough. "Blinded" fails because the other ships rode out the squall in plain sight a mile away, so the crews could see.

P25.author: C
P25.explanation: "Hospital" fits: paintings arrived damaged by the flood, were worked on by restorers in the mine's steady air, and left within a year or two repaired, so the mine was where the museum's injured works were treated. "Depository" fails because the paintings were not simply kept safe and handed back unchanged; they came back cleaned and patched. "Gallery" fails because the restorers' chamber was closed to the public, so nothing was shown. "Dump" fails because every painting went back up repaired, so none was thrown away.

P26.author: E
P26.explanation: The dam turned half a mile of running stream into a pond where the surface barely carried a leaf, so the mill calmed the current: it "stilled" the stream. "Siphoned" means drew water away, but the whole stream spilled over the wheel and went on downstream. "Soured" means fouled the water, but trout fed in the pond as they did above it. "Walled" means hemmed in with walls, but cattle grazed down to the pond's reedy edges.

P27.author: C
P27.explanation: "Dislodged" fits: the ivy's roots worked down the mortar joints, the stones on the ivy half came loose and some fell, and the same stones and mortar on the bare half stayed firm, so the ivy pushed stones out of place. "Fortified" fails because the ivy half is the weaker half, with stones rocking and falling, so the ivy did not strengthen it. "Dried" fails because moisture readings behind the leaves matched those on the bare half. "Etched" fails because the stone faces under the stems were clean; the damage was in the joints, not on the surface.

P28.author: A
P28.explanation: "Bled" fits: a canal draws off two thirds of the river for farms, so the river below shrinks to a third of its width and its side channels go dry each summer; the dam has drained it of most of its water. "Chilled" fails because the release comes from the sunlit surface and warm-water bass still spawn just below the dam. "Churned" fails because what remains is released steadily, so the dam does not stir the river up. "Clogged" fails because the spring floods still pour over the spillway and scour the gravel bars, so silt and plants cannot choke the channel.

P29.author: E
P29.explanation: No tree died in the drought, yet afterward the pines grew slowly for a decade and fell to beetles that healthy pines repel, so the drought left them weakened: it "sapped" the forest. "Winnowed" means removed the weak and left the strong, but the drought killed nothing and the later beetle deaths struck large and small trees alike. "Scorched" means burned or browned, but the needles stayed green through every dry summer. "Toppled" means knocked over, but the dead trees stayed standing until they rotted.

P30.author: D
P30.explanation: Nine days of clear water sank steadily through loose sand, the corn came up pale and short, and the soil's nitrogen fell in the top foot while it rose in the well below, so the flood had "leached" the field, washing its nutrients down out of reach. "Manured" fails because a fertilized field grows darker, taller corn, and this field's corn came up pale beside the higher rows while its topsoil lost nitrogen. "Mulched" fails because water running clear out of a reservoir carries no leaves, straw or other litter to lay a covering over the ground. "Mired" fails because, though the sand was still wet at planting time, the water had been draining down through it, and the corn went in on schedule, which a bogged-down field cannot take.

P31.author: E
P31.explanation: Below the spring, every stone was orange outside but gray or red when cracked, the color the spring's water leaves in a glass, so the river had colored them from outside: it had "stained" them. "Sorted" means separated by size, but the sieved mix of sizes was the same at the cliffs as at the sea. "Stacked" means set one on another, but painted stones moved a mile downstream with each flood and lay wherever they stopped. "Sanded" means worn down by grit, but even at the sea broken pebbles still fit back together edge to edge, so their edges had lost nothing.

P32.author: D
P32.explanation: Residents of the two neighborhoods the yard had divided came in equal numbers on the same evenings and stayed two hours, and friendships between them rose from one tower family in twenty to one in three, so the park is the district's "mixer," where the two communities come together. "Magnet" fails because nearly all visitors walked in from those two neighborhoods, so it drew no one from beyond the district. "Junction" fails because they stayed two hours at the fields and market, so the park was where they were going, not a point they passed through. "Muffler" fails because the lawns slope open to the highway, leaving nothing to absorb its noise.

P33.author: E
P33.explanation: The book keeps every sentence of the notebooks and nothing else, but corrects the mother's spelling and punctuation, so the daughter cleaned up the writing without changing its content: she "tidied" the diary. "Tightened" means made more concise, but every sentence of the notebooks is in the book, down to the weekly egg tallies. "Softened" means toned down, but the curses written after quarrels appear in full. "Spliced" means joined in material from elsewhere, but every sentence in the book is also in the notebooks.

P34.author: A
P34.explanation: "Bedroom" fits: parrotfish arrive at dusk, tuck into crevices and lie still until dawn, then leave to feed elsewhere, so the outcrop is where they spend the night. "Canteen" fails because the fish graze on the reef by day and leave the outcrop's algae to grow a foot long. "Clinic" fails because what protects the fish from parasites is the mucus each one makes for itself; nothing on the outcrop treats them. "Ballroom" fails because the fish arrive one by one and lie still, with no crowd or display.

P35.author: B
P35.explanation: On banded shrubs the flowers stayed whole but fell unfertilized, while on ant shrubs almost every flower an ant had crawled through set a pod, so the ants "pollinated" the shrub. "Patrolled" fails because caterpillars chewed shrubs with and without ants alike and the flowers on banded shrubs came to no harm, so the ants guarded nothing. "Propagated" fails because the pods split where they hung and the seeds fell beneath the parent, so the ants moved no seed. "Parasitized" fails because banded shrubs grew no taller without the ants, while with them the shrub set its pods.

P36.author: A
P36.explanation: "Chased" fits: the wolves ran a mile or more before each kill and took whichever old cow or calf fell behind, so they hunted the herd by pursuit. "Ambushed" fails because an ambush strikes from hiding at close range, and these kills came at the end of long runs on open benches far from cover. "Corralled" fails because the kills fell wherever a straggler dropped back and the herd still ranged over the whole valley floor, so nothing was driven into a confined place. "Cowed" fails because the elk went back to the willow thickets between hunts and browsed them as heavily as before, so the wolves did not frighten them out of their habits.

P37.author: C
P37.explanation: "Herded" fits: the workers moved the aphids off failing shoots onto fresh leaves where they kept feeding, and untended aphids on the other row stayed put and starved, so the ants were steering their stock from poor feeding ground to good. "Drugged" fails because aphids walked just as fast on leaves the ants had crossed as on clean ones, so the ants were not slowing or sedating them; they controlled where the aphids fed by carrying them. "Devoured" fails because the aphids picked up in the ants' jaws were set down alive on young leaves and the population rose all summer. "Garnered" fails because the ants only shifted the aphids from leaf to leaf and left them on the stems, where the frost killed them; nothing was gathered in and stored.

P38.author: B
P38.explanation: The opening says many pieces had been carried off from neighboring towns a century before; the officers took exactly the pieces whose labels named such a town and shipped each crate to the town on its label, so the army had "repatriated" the collection, sending the pieces to the places they were taken from. "Ransacked" fails because the night's work, however hasty it looked, followed a list drawn up beforehand: only marked pieces went, each was numbered, and each was signed for at its destination. "Requisitioned" fails because the army kept nothing for its own use: every crate sailed to the town named on its label. "Ransomed" fails because the city's council was asked for no payment.

P39.author: C
P39.explanation: "Greened" fits: the low dams hold back water that soaks into the meadow, keeping it damp into autumn, and in dry summers the beaver valley stays green while its neighbor turns brown, so the beavers have made their valley greener. "Flooded" fails because the low dams do not spread the creek over the meadow, which has no standing water on it. "Dredged" fails because silt settling behind the dams raises the pond floors each year, filling the bed rather than clearing it. "Deforested" fails because the slopes keep as many aspens as the next valley.

P40.author: E
P40.explanation: The duke paid the monastery to keep the valley's deeds and his treasury chests behind iron doors that opened only on his written order, so it held the valley's valuables secure: a "vault." A "scriptorium" is where books are copied, but clerks read the deeds in place and none was ever copied. A "sanatorium" takes in the sick, but in plague years the valley's sick were turned away from its locked gate. A "tavern" serves travelers food and drink for pay, but travelers on the road bought their wine at the village inn.
